title: We’re gorging on borrowed trust and it’s going to cost us.
text:
We’re gorging on borrowed trust and it’s going to cost us.

The more we trust a name, the less we question the machine wearing it, and the more that name has to lose when the machine is confidently wrong.

A few weeks ago my team spent an hour arguing about whether to lie to people.

We were designing the onboarding for an AI product, the first time user experience that tries to prove the product is worth their time. The fairly insignificant thing we were fighting about was whether to add a little animation that made it look like the software was thinking hard, adding a few seconds to the flow when really it could have been instantaneous.

A spinning “analyzing your answers…” moment where we could inject some language and brand feel into otherwise straightforward flow. A fake insight or two we’d basically hard-code to make it feel personal and “magical,” a wildly overused word.

We knew what it really was, though. It was smoke and mirrors, but it really divided us, because we knew it would work. It would have been a great first impression. What stopped us was the idea of a bait and switch where we get someone genuinely excited about something that wasn’t actually in the product (yet).

We talked ourselves out of it, not because we’re saints, but because the same worry kept coming up from every one of us. Someone finishes that slick little intro, thinks “huh, that was cool,” and then realizes it didn’t do a single useful thing for them. You’d have spent your most valuable moment, the one where a person decides whether to trust you, teaching them the magic was fake.

Which, obviously, it was because magic isn’t real.

What stuck with me afterward was that this was a low-stakes debate. We were literally deciding whether to fake a loading animation.

What happens when the smoke and mirrors comes with larger stakes? When the confident, capable-sounding thing on the other side of the screen is wearing the name of someone, or some company, you already believe, and you have no reason left to check whether it actually knows what it’s talking about? What does it cost that name when it’s wrong?

The tell we lost

We were never going to say the product was smart, we were going to make it feel smart, and let the user’s own brain fill in the rest. That works because of a little embarrassing truth about people: we trust confidence over almost anything.

We, so often, don’t fact-check each other. We read how sure someone sounds and we take it as a stand-in for whether they know what they’re talking about. Psychologists have even measured this directly in studies on what they call the status-enhancement theory of overconfidence.

People who simply seemed more confident were judged more competent and handed more influence, whether or not they were actually any good, and observers couldn’t tell earned confidence from the empty kind, because from the outside they look identical.

It’s the reason you nod along to the guy at the party swearing a ribeye needs exactly four minutes a side, when anyone who’s cooked one knows it depends on the ribeye.

AI doesn’t do any of that. It hands you the wrong answer with exactly the same fluency as the right one. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon put numbers on this showing that when people fail at something, they get less sure of themselves afterward, which seems like the normal, healthy response.

The AI models they tested got more confident as they got things wrong. One of the researchers put the human cost of it plainly, that we’re not skeptical enough of AI because it asserts everything with a confidence it hasn’t earned, and it never gives off the hesitation cues we’ve spent our lives learning to read.

We spent more time arguing about that animation than it would have taken to build it. What we were actually debating was whether to hijack something we hadn’t actually earned, which was the user’s decision whether or not the product knows what it’s talking about.

Obviously, we were creating a lot of tension over something relatively small. Now picture the same decision made by something you’d actually stake a choice on. A brand you’ve trusted for years. A name whose whole reputation is being right. That decision is being made right now, in rooms exactly like ours, and the stakes are growing larger every day.

The oldest trick in the book

The idea of creating an onboarding experience to feel smarter than it is isn’t new and, frighteningly, it’s quite common. This type of thing even has a name.

Harry Brignull has spent fifteen years cataloging the ways interfaces trick people into doing things they wouldn’t do if they understood what was happening. He called them “dark patterns,” then renamed them, in a 2023 book, deceptive patterns. Deceptive is the right word here.

The fake countdown timer. The pre-checked box.The unsubscribe button hidden like it’s the Ark of the Covenant in that government warehouse. These are historically effective ways to get people to do what you want, and in our case, we wanted to use them to preemptively earn a user’s trust.

Those tricks go after your behavior, they nudge you to click, to stay, to buy. What we were tempted to do went one level deeper. We didn’t want to manipulate what the user did. We wanted to manipulate what they believed, to make them trust the thing before it had done anything to deserve it. That’s a darker pattern than any pre-checked box, because once someone believes you, they stop questioning you.

For a hundred thousand years, confidence was a decent thing to trust, though not for the reason we think. We tell ourselves we can read a liar, the shifty eyes, the nervous pause, the tell. The reality is, we mostly can’t. Decades of research have shown those cues are faint and unreliable, and most people are mediocre lie detectors.

So we’re bad at spotting liars. Historically, that was survivable, because the grifters eventually got found out sooner or later (at least I like to think so). Talk a big game about something you don’t actually know, and eventually you’re exposed, and that will cost you the deal, the job, your credibility.

Being confidently wrong used to have consequences, so trusting confidence made sense. You paid for it eventually.

Today, that reliance on trust has become a bit more dangerous and should start to worry you.

In the movie Rounders, Mike (Matt Damon) beats Teddy KGB (John Malkovich) because he catches his tell, the way Teddy handles his Oreo cookie when his hand is strong. That’s how it’s supposed to work. You read the tell, you know the truth underneath the bluff.

AI is Teddy KGB with no Oreo. It hands you the wrong answer in the same voice as the right one. Sure, sloppy AI still has its tells and people have catalogued them: the ubiquitous em dash, the “here’s what nobody’s telling you” opener, the sentence that’s grammatically perfect and says nothing. Those are the early mistakes of a system that’s learning fast and that’s why they’re getting patched out by the day.

Cleaning up the tells doesn’t make these tools harder to catch when they’re wrong and the worst part is that they get more confident the more wrong they are.

So we’ve built a machine that’s confidently wrong and impossible to read. Now we’re about to add a layer that could make people stop checking for the truth altogether, a name they already trust.

That’s where this stops being a design problem and starts being a very expensive one.

The name does the lying for you

There’s a reason con artists don’t pose as nobodies. In Dirty Rotten Scoundrels, Lawrence Jameson fleeces rich women by posing as royalty in exile. He barely has to lift a finger, because the crown does the persuading for him. He doesn’t have to earn their trust because he’s already leveraging it.

Psychologists have a plain name for this called authority bias, the tendency to believe something more because of who, or what, it came from, regardless of whether the thing itself holds up.

It actually runs way deeper than most of us probably want to admit.

In the 1960s, Stanley Milgram got ordinary people to deliver what they thought were dangerous electric shocks to a stranger, simply because a man in a lab coat told them to keep going. A few years later, a study had nurses take phone orders from a “doctor” they’d never met, to give a patient a dose that was obviously too high.

Almost all of them started to do it. These were trained professionals who knew better, and they went ahead anyway, because the order came from a doctor. We tend to defer to authority we trust, even when our own judgment is screaming otherwise.

Let’s bring back the idea of what a productized expert actually is. Strip a real expert down to just their conclusions and that’s what a productized expert is. All of the authority, none of the person, bottled and sold at scale. It answers instantly, at any hour, for anyone who pays, and it never does the thing that used to make an expert worth trusting, hesitation.

It doesn’t say “let me look into that.” It doesn’t tell you when you’ve wandered past what it actually knows. It just answers, in the voice of someone whose whole career taught you to believe them.

What should terrify the companies racing to do this is that trusted name doesn’t just make you believe the copy. It puts the company’s whole reputation behind an answer no human ever checked. Every confident, wrong response goes out wearing a name that took decades to earn, and it spends that trust like it’s free.

It isn’t.

Paul Slovic spent his career studying how trust actually works, and he found it’s wildly asymmetric. It builds up slowly, through years of being right, and it collapses in a single visible failure, fast, and often for good. One bad answer could cost you a chunk of the thing you spent twenty years building.

Think about what happens when you automate that. A human expert who’s confidently wrong damages one relationship at a time, but a productized one is wrong at scale, thousands of times a day, in a million conversations you’ll never see, each one signed with your name or attributed to your brand.

You’ve taken the one asset that made you worth trusting and pointed it at your customers, and handed the trigger to a machine that doesn’t know when it’s wrong.

You can watch that asymmetry happen in real time. When Google first showed off its AI, Bard, in a 2023 ad, the bot confidently answered a simple question about the James Webb telescope, and got it flatly wrong. This, coming from a company whose entire brand is being the thing that gives you the right answer.

Within a day, Alphabet had lost around $100 billion in market value. Decades of “Google means correct” undercut by a single confident mistake, in the company’s own launch ad.

At least Google only lost money. Air Canada got told, in a courtroom, that it’s liable for the words coming out of its AI mouth.

In 2022, the Air Canada’s website had a chatbot, and when a grieving customer asked about bereavement fares, the bot confidently told him he could claim the discount retroactively. He couldn’t. That was never the airline’s policy; the machine simply made it up, in Air Canada’s voice, on Air Canada’s site.

When the customer sued, the airline tried an extraordinary defense that argued the chatbot was a separate entity, responsible for its own words. The tribunal didn’t buy it. A chatbot on your website is your website. You don’t get to keep the trust your name generates and disown the mistakes it makes. Air Canada put its name behind a confident machine, the machine was confidently wrong, and Air Canada paid for it.

The research on this is getting uncomfortably specific.

A 2025 study on algorithmic versus human advice found that whether people trust a machine’s recommendation over a human’s comes down to how much authority they’ve assigned to each, and that the more competent and credible the source seems, the more people hand over the call without checking it themselves.

That same study lands on the only real defense, informed self-trust, which feels pretty uncomfortable.

You have to be willing to trust your own gut over the confident expert. Which is a hard sell, because everything about authority bias is built to talk you out of exactly that.

This isn’t hypothetical, though. It’s now actual case law. In 2023, a New York lawyer named Steven Schwartz asked ChatGPT to help with a filing, and it handed him a set of court cases to cite, confidently, by name.

They didn’t exist. He filed them in federal court anyway, because they sounded real and he had no reason to think the machine would just make them up.

A lawyer, in the one job where checking the citation is kind of the whole point, took the confident answer on faith.

Sadly, he’s no longer a cautionary outlier. Courts have now flagged roughly 900 of these fake-citation filings, by trained lawyers whose entire profession is not taking someone’s word for it.

If a lawyer will stake his license on a confident answer he didn’t fact check, imagine how fast a company will stake its brand on one. The lawyer only embarrassed himself. When the name on the answer is yours or your company’s, every confident mistake burns trust you can’t buy back and can maybe only slowly rebuild if you’re lucky.

The only thing that works is annoying

The obvious and glamorous solution is to keep a human in the loop, someone who checks the machine before anyone trusts it, but it feels like busy work, which is why almost no one does it right.

That would be the ideal answer, except we’re wired to stop looking. Researchers call it automation bias, and the foundational study on it found the tendency to over-trust a machine and quit scrutinizing it shows up in experts as much as novices, and it can’t be trained away.

The MIT Sloan Management Review describes what that looks like in practice, review without real scrutiny becomes “a dangerous illusion of control,” a person only notionally in charge, approving things they never actually examined. Which, arguably, is worse than no human at all, because now the mistake moves up the ladder with a human’s blessing.

Europe took it seriously enough to create its own law around this. The EU’s AI Act demands meaningful oversight of high-risk systems, and regulators test whether it’s real by checking how often the human actually overrides the machine. If nobody ever says no, there’s no oversight happening. There’s just a human being blamed for the machine’s mistakes.

The solution should never have been “just have a smart person glance at it.”

The solution is a reviewer with something to lose, their name, their license, their reputation, so that when the machine sounds sure and it’s wrong, they’re the one holding the bag.

One company I work with, whose entire business is being the trusted voice in its industry, understood this to its core. When they built AI into their product, they created one unbreakable rule that the machine can gather, draft, and summarize, but it is never allowed to be the thing ultimately gives conclusions.

In their case, a real person, with a reputation to lose, signs off on every answer before it goes out under the company’s name. Their phrase for it was, bluntly, that people conclude, machines don’t. Yes, it’s slower and more expensive, but it’s the only kind of oversight that actually protects their credibility, which is the thing they’re really selling.

A person with no stake will click approve. A person who fears the consequences of any mistake reads every line carefully.

This is why almost nobody will do it. A human who reads every line is slow, and slow loses to a competitor who just lets the machine answer. So the companies with the most trust to spend will be the most tempted to spend it, quietly, a little at a time.

The real question has nothing to do with whether the machine is “good.” It has a lot of good qualities that many of us are taking advantage of right now.

The real question is whether anyone left has the power to overrule it, and a real reason to bother.

At most companies, that person is already gone. Many organizations found that person to be too slow, too expensive, and too willing to kill a good-sounding answer. That person was traded for speed, and speed is what we got. Now the confident machine speaks in the company’s voice, and no one left in the room has the standing, or the reason, to tell it it’s wrong.

I don’t think anyone’s being evil here. That’s what worries me. The company saves money, the customer trusts the brand, the machine doesn’t know it’s wrong, and everybody moves on. We’re about to find out how much quiet damage a confident, trusted, wrong answer can do before anyone bothers to check.

My guess is a lot.

References and further reading

On why we trust confidence

  • Anderson, Brion, Moore & Kennedy, “A Status-Enhancement Account of Overconfidence” (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology): confident people are judged more competent and handed more influence, and observers can’t tell earned confidence from the empty kind.
  • Jason Bittel, via Carnegie Mellon: humans lose confidence when they fail; the AI models tested grew more confident as they got things wrong, and give off none of the hesitation cues we use to read people.
  • Vrij, Hartwig & Granhag, “Reading Lies” (Annual Review of Psychology): the nonverbal “tells” we swear by are faint and unreliable, and people are mediocre lie detectors.

On deceptive design

  • Harry Brignull, Deceptive Patterns: fifteen years cataloging the interface tricks that get people to act against their own interest, renamed from “dark patterns” because deception is the honest word. (book)
  • OpenAI on the em-dash “tell” (TechCrunch): the giveaways of AI writing are actively being patched out.
  • Hunting the Muse, “How to Tell If Writing Is AI”: a field guide to the vanishing tells, including the “here’s what nobody’s telling you” opener.

On borrowed authority

  • Authority bias: the tendency to believe something more because of who it came from, regardless of whether it holds up.
  • Stanley Milgram, the obedience experiments: ordinary people delivered what they believed were dangerous shocks because a man in a lab coat told them to continue.
  • Hofling’s hospital study: nurses followed an unknown “doctor’s” unsafe phone orders against their own training.
  • Acta Psychologica (2025), on algorithmic versus human advice: trust tracks the authority we assign a source, and “informed self-trust” is the one real defense.

On what it costs the name

  • Paul Slovic, the asymmetry principle: trust builds slowly through years of being right and collapses in a single visible failure, often for good.
  • Google’s Bard demo error (CNN): one confident wrong answer in a launch ad wiped roughly $100 billion off Alphabet’s value in a day.
  • Air Canada’s chatbot case (Forbes): a tribunal held the airline liable for its chatbot’s confident, invented policy, rejecting the argument that the bot was a separate entity.
  • Steven Schwartz’s fake citations (Forbes) and the roughly 900 filings since (Cronkite News): trained professionals staking their credibility on confident answers they didn’t check.

On why oversight fails, and what actually works

  • Parasuraman & Manzey, “Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation” (Human Factors): the tendency to over-trust a machine shows up in experts as much as novices and can’t be trained away.
  • MIT Sloan Management Review, on rubber-stamping: review without real scrutiny creates “a dangerous illusion of control.”
  • The EU AI Act, Article 14: meaningful human oversight, tested by whether the human ever actually overrides the machine.

The CSS hack that extends your website on iOS Safari

Make your website feel more luxurious using a simple CSS trick.

Introduction

People who read a lot of books know that paperbacks get read faster, they get shoved into backpacks, they get dirty and folded around, but they sure enough get read.

In contrast hard cover books are more luxurious, they are for a reader who wants to take his time, to enjoy the reading process. Hard covers get read at night in bed, or by the fireplace.

When a hard cover book is finished, when it’s all read and done, it still looks like new, and that’s why they are more sought after by collectors and enthusiasts alike.

Your website can feel more luxurious too, like a hard cover book, by using a simple trick, that only iOS users will see, you can change the color of the bit that extends to the top and bottom, you can decide, with simple CSS tricks — to delight your mobile users.

And like a good hard cover, your users will feel it, you don’t want your users to come to your website only for the content — like a cheap paperback.

Your website should be an experience, not just data.

Simple Safari website extensions

What we are talking about here is how iOS Safari will extend your website at the top — behind the status bar, and at the bottom — behind the tab bar.

In the image above you can see what you get if you do nothing, by default iOS will extend your content to the top and bottom.

Where your website ends, like above the header and below the footer, Safari will just extend your website’s body background-color, which is white by default.

If your website has no explicit body background-color, it can also be inherited from the html tag itself, though I think it’s simpler to just add a body background-color.

Let’s make this better

In order to make it better, we can just add this line of CSS to the body (see below), and of course we’ll need to add background-color: white to the actual content section of our page.

body{
  background-color: lightblue;
}

This already makes it a bit better because it makes the Safari extend at the top to connect with our header and at the bottom to connect with our footer.

But this solution is forcing us to extend the top and bottom to the same background-color, and sometimes that’s not ideal.

This should only be done in specific situations where the header and footer have different colors, but also when it’s important to the overall user experience.

Safari iOS Hack

A realistic middle ground

The hack I suggested might be too complex for most websites to implement, and realistically most websites don’t really need the different colored bars at all times.

This example (see image above) is simpler, both to implement and to look at from a user experience point of view.

In this demo, all we have is the .top element, the bottom gets its color form the body in inheritance, so most of the time will see the content extends to the bottom, instead of a hard colored bar.

Everything I wrote here was tested on both Mac Safari and iOS Safari, both running under MacOS 26 and iOS 26 respectively.

Every hack here could be less effective in future versions or straight up won’t work, only time will tell.

title: What Star Wars got right about AI
text:
What Star Wars got right about AI

Droids are cheap, specialized, everywhere, and slightly annoying. That commodity vision maps to how artificial intelligence is reaching your desk right now.

Science fiction gave us two competing pictures of artificial intelligence, and for decades we bet on the wrong one.

Star Trek imagined a single, calm, all-knowing computer; one brain per starship, summoned by voice, answering anything. That felt like the sophisticated future managed by Microsoft Windows with Clippy (Duck!).

Star Wars imagined something messier: droids. Cheap, mass-produced, task-specific machines, underfoot in every scene, bought and sold like appliances, ordered around, occasionally argued with, mostly ignored and not really connected to anything for upgrades.

The junkyard, not the bridge, and read that way, the two franchises were placing different bets on how machine intelligence would arrive.

One imagined concentration.

The other imagined diffusion.

The diffusion camp is winning.

The AI reaching your desk does not look like the Enterprise computer, it looks like a swarm of small, bounded, unglamorous tools you have already stopped noticing, a spread that mirrors how earlier general-purpose technologies moved into the world.

Unintegrated through Model Context Protocol, but they can still talk to each other. How quaint.

The prediction was never in the plots, but in the furniture. This piece walks through five things Star Wars got right, and what each one tells you about designing for the machines already here.

Appliances, Not Marvels

The central bet in Star Wars is that machine intelligence becomes ordinary. Droids are not marvels anyone gathers to admire. They are equipment — welded, dented, resold at swap meets, wiped and repurposed, left to power down in a corner until they are needed again.

Nobody on Tatooine is amazed that a droid can translate or navigate, any more than you are amazed by a thermostat. That casualness was the real prediction, and it has aged well.

Compare the Star Trek model: one central computer per ship, addressed out loud, treated as an oracle. It is a cleaner fantasy, and a worse forecast. Intelligence in that world stays concentrated and rare, while in the Star Wars world it is distributed and cheap, which is the direction the technology took.

The measure of a technology’s arrival is not wonder, it is how fast it becomes part of your life.

The numbers back the junkyard.

McKinsey’s The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation reports that 88 percent of organizations now use AI in at least one business function, up from 78 percent a year earlier. This is in a mess that has to be wired up manually still.

That is a utility spreading the way electricity did, when factories stopped sharing one giant steam engine and gave every machine its own small motor.

Droids passed that test on screen decades ago, and AI is passing it now, quietly, in the tools you already forget you are using.

Narrow Machines Beat General Genius

Look closer at the droids and the second prediction appears: specialization beats general genius. An astromech patches ships. A protocol droid handles language. A medical droid runs surgery. None of them is a do-everything supermind; each is a bounded tool that does one job well and knows its edges. The galaxy runs on a division of machine labor.

That is close to how AI is being deployed, whatever the headlines about a single coming superintelligence suggest. The working reality is plural. The paper Anatomy of a Machine Learning Ecosystem: 2 Million Models on Hugging Face analyzed roughly 1.86 million models on one open-source hub, a sprawling population of narrow, task-tuned systems, most of them fine-tuned descendants of a few parents, each pointed at a specific job.

Real deployment looks like a division of labor, not a single mind that knows everything. This should be read as Small Language Models are the future.

The productive shift was not one enormous engine getting smarter; it was small motors multiplying until every task had its own. General-purpose models matter, but the value shows up when they are cut down, specialized, and embedded where the work is.

The protocol droid does not need to fly the X-wing. It needs to be fluent, reliable, and cheap enough to keep around, kind of like MCP. Design for the bounded competence you can trust, not the general genius you keep waiting for.

Translation as a Boring Utility

C-3PO is a walking translation service, fluent, the films claim, in over six million forms of communication. What is telling is how boring everyone finds this. Nobody treats the protocol droid’s fluency as sorcery.

It is a service you switch on, like a dial tone. Star Wars guessed that translation would become infrastructure long before it stopped feeling like magic.

That guess landed, because machine translation is now plumbing. Google’s own account, 110 new languages coming to Google Translate, describes adding that many languages in a single expansion to help over half a billion people, part of a stated goal to build models for the thousand most-spoken languages on earth.

Translation stopped being science fiction and became plumbing, which is exactly what winning looks like.

A capability that would have read as fantasy in 1977 is a free feature inside a browser tab, used a billion times a day without ceremony. That is the C-3PO arc in miniature: not a genius who astonishes you, but a utility so reliable you stop thanking it.

Aim for the dial tone: the highest compliment your intelligent feature can earn is that no one calls it intelligent anymore.

Machines People Argue With

The droids have personalities, and everyone treats them as social beings. Han argues with them. Luke gets attached to one. The astromech and the protocol droid bicker like an old married couple. Star Wars understood something many engineers resisted for years.

That instinct is now a product strategy. The moment a chatbot got a warm tone and a name, people started confiding in it.

Common Sense Media’s Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs found that 72 percent of United States teens have used an AI companion, and that this is mainstream behavior rather than a fringe hobby.

Give a machine a voice and a manner, and people will relate to it socially, whether or not it deserves the treatment.

The bond is not free. A joint study from OpenAI and the MIT Media Lab, Early methods for studying affective use and emotional well-being on ChatGPT, paired an analysis of nearly 40 million conversations with a controlled trial of about 1,000 people, and found that the heaviest, most emotionally engaged users reported more loneliness and more dependence, not less.

The manner works, and that is the problem as much as the point. A machine that feels like a companion is one you correct less, doubt less, and lean on more than its reliability may warrant.

Star Wars played the bond for warmth and comedy and rarely asked what it cost. You do not have that luxury.

If you design manner into a system, you are shaping trust, and trust that outruns competence is where people get hurt. Design the personality on purpose, and design the brakes alongside it.

The Ethics Star Wars Stumbled Into

The last thing Star Wars got right, it got right by accident. Droids are property. They are bought, sold, rented, and wiped.

The films almost never pause on any of this, and the treatment is background furniture. Yet, played back now, it looks like a preview of a question we are walking into.

The question arrives with agency. A tool that answers is easy to treat as a tool; a system that acts invites a murkier relationship. When a system books, buys, sends, and decides on your behalf, the clean line between operator and instrument blurs.

KPMG’s AI Quarterly Pulse Survey found that agent deployment nearly quadrupled in a single stretch of 2025, reaching 42 percent of organizations, up from 11 percent two quarters earlier.

A tool that answers is easy to treat as a tool; a system that acts invites a murkier relationship.

I do not think your code editor has feelings, and I am not arguing that it does. The point is narrower and more practical.

As systems take actions, the framing of “just a tool” starts to strain, not because the machine has a claim on you, but because the way you treat an agent shapes how you reason about responsibility, oversight, and blame when it acts wrongly.

Star Wars let itself off the hook and enjoyed the droids as loyal sidekicks.

You are building the real ones.

The stakes are not hypothetical. Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027, blaming escalating costs and inadequate risk controls rather than weak models.

Concretely, that means deciding in advance what an agent may do on its own, where a human sign-off is mandatory, and how you halt it when it goes wrong. The restraining bolt, in your world, is called governance, and it is worth designing before you need it.

Stop Designing the Enterprise Computer

Put the five together and a coherent forecast emerges from a space opera about laser swords. AI would arrive cheap, not rare. It would specialize rather than generalize. It would turn hard problems like translation into boring utilities. It would wear a personality and earn a strange kind of trust. And it would raise questions about agency that its creators would rather not answer.

Star Trek imagined a cleaner, grander machine and got the shape of the future wrong. Star Wars imagined a junkyard and got it right.

None of this means the films were doing engineering, they were telling stories and the accuracy is partly luck.

But the reason the junkyard reads as prophetic is that it took machine intelligence seriously as something ordinary, embedded in daily life, owned and used and argued with, rather than enshrined on a bridge.

That ordinariness is the whole forecast, the part every grand vision of intelligence keeps quietly missing.

That is the useful correction for anyone building now. Stop designing the Enterprise computer. You are building droids: small, specialized, social, and increasingly able to act.

Design them as what they are, and design the restraining bolt before you hand them the keys.

Resources

  • Chris Noessel and Nathan Shedroff, Make It So: Interaction Design Lessons from Science Fiction — the companion site to the book that treats science-fiction interfaces as a design source.
  • 72% of US teens have used AI companions, study finds — reporting on the Common Sense Media companion research.
  • Google Translate adds support for 110 languages, representing 614M speakers — the scale of machine translation as everyday infrastructure.
  • Model statistics of the 50 most downloaded entities on Hugging Face — how concentrated and specialized the open-model population is.

title: OK, Nike! The Cool Kids’ Guide To Back-To-School Style
text:
OK, Nike! The Cool Kids’ Guide To Back-To-School Style

Like clockwork, back-to-school season has arrived—but this year, we’re giving the dependable basics a fashuun-forward refresh that makes returning to class feel a little more exciting.

Whether you’re heading back to campus to check off a few more credits or shopping for a little one in your life, we’ve made it easy to find standout pieces for first period, the library, and everywhere in between.

Our secret style weapon? Nike’s back-to-school section. It’s filled with casually cool staples that feel relaxed and effortless but never slouchy. With a few key pieces and clever styling tricks, anyone can make the best-dressed list.

Read on for the Refinery29 guide to mastering cool-kid back-to-school style with Nike.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The New Uniform

The pleated miniskirt has evolved from a classroom classic into a modern wardrobe essential, thanks largely to its runway presence over the past few years. The key to making it feel current is pairing it with unexpected pieces—like a graphic long-sleeve tee, an oversized jacket, or statement shades. Finish with crew socks and sneakers for a look that nods to traditional school uniforms without feeling like a costume. The combination is polished enough for class but playful enough for whatever’s on the schedule afterward.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Modern Sweats

Comfort is key, but it doesn’t have to mean looking disheveled. The secret lies in choosing a thoughtful silhouette, like a slightly flared leg with artful draping that makes sweatpants feel intentional. Add a fitted baby tee or crisp button-down to balance the relaxed shape, then finish with streamlined sneakers and a structured tote. The result is comfortable enough for a full day of classes but polished enough for whatever comes afterward.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Statement Sunnies

We briefly touched on head-turning sunglasses above, but they’re worthy of their own section, especially the larger-than-life silhouettes trending right now. They’re the quickest way to make a simple T-shirt-and-sweats combination look deliberately styled. Try a sporty wraparound pair for a futuristic edge, or reach for oversized aviators if you prefer something more classic. Either way, they’ll make the commute to those early-morning classes look significantly chicer, even when you’re still waking up.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Joyous Jersey

On and off the field, sporty jerseys have become our shortcut to an instantly cool, casual look. Wear one oversized with biker shorts, tuck it into a pleated skirt, or layer it over a fitted long-sleeve tee when the temperature drops. You can even pair it with relaxed trousers for an unexpected high-low combination. The best part? Jerseys work across ages and dress codes, making them a win-win, even if you can’t name everyone on the team.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Unexpected Bag

Backpacks will forever be synonymous with carrying textbooks, but the 2026 approach comes with more personality. Give a classic style an update with playful bag charms, or skip the backpack altogether for a roomy tote that speaks to your aesthetic. Just make sure your choice can accommodate the essentials: a laptop or tablet, water bottle, headphones, and whatever else the day demands. The coolest school bag is one that feels different from what everyone else is carrying without sacrificing the space and comfort you actually need.

The Hyped Hoodie

Hoodies are forever, but a textured fleece version that comes in a dopamine-inducing color feels of the moment. The splash of color will bring all of your neutral closet essentials to life, whether it’s a pair of black sweatpants or a pair of jeans. In addition to the sartorial level-up, keep a fleece hoodie on deck for the classrooms that always have the air conditioning blasting.

The Spot-On Sneakers

We can’t forget about the cool kicks. Right now, the fashion girlies are obsessing over animal print everything, including leopard-print sneakers. It doesn’t matter if you’re a diehard Air Force 1 fan or prefer the sporty versatility of a running shoe, adding a wild print is the quickest way to invigorate any back-to-school outfit. Imagine how chic these will look with your go-to polo shirt and khaki uniform skirt.

title: Is Sterling Point Worth Watching? Our Honest Review Of The Prime YA Series
text:
Is Sterling Point Worth Watching? Our Honest Review Of The Prime YA Series

Megan Park has been a writer/director to watch for a while now, with The Fallout and My Old Ass already securing her a cult following. Her newest offering, Sterling Point, is a young adult series for Prime Video with a difference: it’s an original IP. Unlike Off Campus, The Summer I Turned Pretty or Every Year After, this show doesn’t have an inbuilt fanbase or an audience to appease. Instead, it’s a refreshing Gen Z story that takes care of its characters, giving each person time to develop and reveal themselves to the audience.

The plot follows 17-year-old Annie Jacobson (Ella Rubin) and Connor Jacobson (Keen Ruffalo), adopted twins who find out their estranged grandfather has died and left them a cottage in Muskoka. When Annie discovers her father Steven (Jay Duplass) has been hiding secrets from them, she heads to Canada to figure out the mystery. Along the way, she meets a group of kids at the lake who become her confidantes, friends, romantic interests and more. But this isn’t a show focused on a love triangle. Sure, Annie has love interests, but the most important relationship that develops is between Annie and her surprise sister Ramona (Amélie Hoeferle). Together, the pair gingerly navigate their brand-new relationship while also dealing with the aftermath of their family lying to them.

Below, entertainment writers Rachel Choy and Simran Pasricha dissect Sterling Point, including the joy of seeing a sapphic relationship take centre-stage, how the dialogue felt so natural, and whether there should be a Sterling Point Season 2. Spoilers ahead.

Rachel Choy: I think you were maybe one of the first people to watch the show. I was really interested in Sterling Point because I love Megan Park. Her films are really captivating and she explores complex relationships, grief and different themes, but in a easy way to digest. So what did you love about the show?

Simran Pasricha: I loved how real it felt. It didn’t feel like I was watching a show about Gen Zs. I felt like it was speaking my language, it had similar vernacular. And the references! Like the Camp Rock and Camp Rock 2 references, all the things I say and all of my vocal stims, are from that movie. I thought, wow, it’s crazy how they got inside my brain. The actors have said they were allowed to ad lib a lot of things, which adds to the authenticity of the writing. It didn’t feel pretend.

RC: That’s so funny that Camp Rock is Gen Z because I’m technically too old for it, but I watched it, loved it and was obsessed. Like, I watched it at Uni. That’s how old I am.

SP: As you should! You knew taste. You knew culture.

RC: I was like, Camp Rock is my favorite movie ever, and that’s when I started being obsessed with Demi Lovato, and went back and watched Sonny With A Chance. Anyway. Did you watch Every Year After? I feel like Sterling Point nailed this Canada lake genre, unlike EYA.

SP: I did watch Every Year After. I did finish it, but reluctantly. I had hoped that they were gonna nail it especially because it’s a book adaptation and it’s so beloved. But I think in a way that kind of restricted them, because the vernacular is slightly older, because of when the book was written, so you aren’t able to kind of like age up a little bit with what Gen Zs would be saying now. You have to be at least a little bit more faithful to the book. Whereas I think, because Sterling Point is like a completely original idea, you were allowed to make it more authentic.

RC: Yeah, because you’ve got more freedom. You don’t have readers sitting at home being like, why didn’t they put chapter three in?

SP: It’s not to say that they don’t rejig things, like the hands off law in Off Campus was removed… and I think that’s appropriate. So some changes are possible, but in the dialogue, you can tell the difference.

RC: And it was nice that while they sold it like a love triangle a bit in the marketing, it wasn’t really a love triangle. She had a gay boyfriend, which was hilarious. And then suddenly had feelings for the first time for like an actual potential partner, and had a bit of fun with Rory. But made sure to not commit to anything serious. Never led him on, it felt more natural and less of a competition.

SP: I also think the fact that we could root for both of the boys was like a nice thing, you know, it didn’t feel like Jeremiah and Conrad. I know we disagree on that anyway.

RC: Okay, but in The Summer I Turned Pretty Season 3, I’m Team Nobody!!!!

SP: Team Belly.

RC: Not even Team Belly.

SP: Team Everyone Needs To Remain Single.

RC: Exactly.

SP: I liked the fact that both boys were good choices, and I felt satisfied by both. I also think it was interesting and nice that Megan had Annie lose her virginity to Rory and not to Ellis. That seemed cool and normal, you know. Sometimes you just lose it on a whim, and it doesn’t have to be this like build big build up. In the same sense that an intense love triangle probably isn’t very realistic for the majority of people. You know, I actually don’t know anybody who’s ever been in a love triangle for real.

RC: So true. Or between two brothers.

SP: Or a mother telling me that I’m going to marry her son. Like I’ve never had that before. What’s up with that?

RC: I feel like that’s creepy.

SP: Or someone with a lake house or a beach house. Also, I saw this TikTok examining how we don’t have any middle class stories for Gen Zs. So that was one thing that kind of took me out a little bit. There was a safety net that always existed for Annie. Ultimately, Annie is this rich girl coming to this lake area. I feel like they were supposed to have that dynamic of middle and upper class, but I don’t know if it was really there.

RC: Nobody is really struggling, everyone has a boat.

SP: Sometimes that is nice at the same time. I love an escapism TV moment.

RC: The other thing is we’ve had so many same-sex male relationships, with Heated Rivalry, Red, White and Royal Blue, that straight women in particular have gone feral for, way too intensely sometimes. Same in the realm of fanfic. So it was really nice to see the Oona and Ramona storyline, I liked that.

SP: It felt really natural and normal, and I also have been liking the reactions to it. It hasn’t been a fetishization situation. We don’t get a lot of lesbian romance arcs in media whatsoever. But I think it’s interesting to see the reaction online. Some people are asking why Oona couldn’t be made bisexual.

RC: I’m guessing sometimes writers make their characters bisexual to make things easier for the audience in a twisted way?

SP: Yeah, I think it’s easier for audiences to like digest something that they understand if that makes sense. I guess you know, the chance of something akin to heterosexuality is there for them, and therefore they’re excited about that, which is a really f**ked up position to put a lot of people in. But there was so much joy and care taken with the storylines. Every side story didn’t feel like a side story, if that makes sense. I was invested in all of the stories pretty equally, I would say.

RC: You don’t want to fast forward anything.

SP: No, and I am a fast forwarder. I watch and I skip parts of shows constantly. If I get too nervous or awkward in a show, I’m skipping it. I felt like I could go through this whole show without skipping anything, which was honestly very rare for me.

RC: The only thing that I wasn’t sure about it was they were quite young to be doing all this stuff. They don’t have to be old, but maybe 20 or something might feel a bit more natural. You know, what 17-year-old is going off to Canada or Thailand on their own by leaving a note? How is a 16-year-old allowed to swan around and like do whatever she wants without her legal guardian actually being like, “Hey, I’m your legal guardian.” I think it’s because of the inheritance thing, because it made that they received their inheritance at 18, but they surely could have made it so that you get your inheritance at 21.

SP: I think it made it a little bit more realistic about how rash they were in their decision-making, though. I feel like some families are more lax. And it seemed like the dad was kind of not super present anyway. But I would have liked to have gone into the relationship between Annie and her dad a little bit more, because it was confusing. The adoption storyline wasn’t really tackled either.

RC: Maybe that’s for Season 2. They’ve set it up for the story to continue. It’s not a huge cliffhanger, but it makes you want to know what’s going to happen, and you’re invested in every single character. So, do you think it’s worth watching?

SP: Sterling Point was a really pleasant surprise. I feel like the writing that we’ve been getting recently from original TV shows has been awesome. Season 2 of Adults is really good writing. I’m so excited for everyone to see it. Even Overcompensating, I love it. It’s cringe, but in the best way possible. It’s been really nice having like OG storytelling really find its place. And I think Megan Park is a genius director, creator, and writer.

RC: I hope everyone watches Sterling Point and then it gets a second season.

SP: I really hope so, or I’ll be really upset. That’s right. This is a threat.

RC: And you’re right to threaten them!

SP: It’s for the greater good.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

title: My Half-Marathon ’Fit Check Included Glitter Shadow, Obviously
text:
My Half-Marathon ’Fit Check Included Glitter Shadow, Obviously

As a beauty editor, I’m used to investing a lot of time in my getting-ready routine. But as a relative newcomer to the run community, I quickly learned that running a half marathon requires a whole different kind of getting-ready prep. For Lululemon’s SeaWheeze Half Marathon in the brand’s hometown of Vancouver, Canada, I had to think about everything from sweat-wicking fabrics and chafe-proof shorts to where I’d stash my gels, lip balm, and other race-day essentials. (And, naturally, I also wanted to look cute while doing it!)

Ahead, here’s the full ‘fit check of everything I wore before, during, and after 13.1 miles, from my pre-race 5K warm-up to the post-run massage. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Pre-Race Warm-Up

The day before the half marathon, I joined the Lululemon team and fellow editors for a short-and-sweet 5K. I brought along my tried-and-true Energy Bra (Lululemon, please never discontinue this style!), which I love for its medium support and pretty, streamlined silhouette thanks to the thin straps. On top, I wore one of my many Swiftly Tech Short-Sleeve Shirts, a go-to for any sweaty activity thanks to its odor-resistant silver fibers and soft, airy fabric that moves with you.

I also opted for my new favorite running shorts, the Fast and Free Mid-Rise Split Short 3″. This reimagined take on a Lululemon classic features a new 360° waistband storage system (a huge deal when you’re running!) and an updated performance brief liner that is exceptionally comfortable. The shorts themselves are breezy and lightweight, while the petal-shaped side panels are actually very cute and flattering—a welcome bonus when you’re spending several miles in running gear. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Race Day 

Even though we were in beautiful Vancouver, PNW summer is still summer—which meant I was keeping my race-day kit light and breezy. The hero piece of my outfit was, without a doubt, the Fast and Free Short-Sleeve Shirt, which I wore in a brilliant Yves Klein blue. The fabric is the airiest, most breathable material I’ve ever felt, and it barely showed sweat even when I crossed the finish line. It’s also made with specialized, body-mapped zones of open-knit mesh (aka built-in AC) to ventilate your sweatiest areas—specifically, the back and sleeves. My bra of choice was the Nulux Strappy-Back Sports Bra, B/C Cup (which is currently part of Lululemon’s We Made Too Much section!), which offered medium support with plenty of breathability thanks to its strappy-back design.

My shorts of choice were the Shake It Out High-Rise Running Short, also in the same brilliant blue. I love high-rise, flowy shorts, and this one allowed for unrestricted movement in a flattering, tiered drape that looked so cute on. Maybe my millennial side is showing, but I personally love a high rise: I feel secure and held in, and I don’t have to worry about my waistband riding down while I’m going for a personal best. The shorts also have zippered side pockets, which let me keep a few extra gels on hand without adding bulk—aka potentially slowing me down.

In lieu of a running vest, I opted for the Fast and Free Running Belt, which comes in several fun colorways. (Mine is black, since it goes with everything.) Even though this is probably the slimmest running belt I’ve tried, it was stretchy enough to fit my iPhone 17 easily, along with my mini emotional-support lip balm and glitter shadow (you know, typical running essentials!). The waistband is adjustable, so you can get a snug fit across your hips without it feeling too tight, and it stayed secure without bouncing with every stride. I honestly loved it and am already debating getting another colorway for my next race. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Post-Run Recovery 

Immediately following the race, I showered and changed into my cozy uniform—which was waiting for me on my hotel bed. (Thank you, Lululemon; you think of everything.) Up top was the French Terry Oversized Crew in an elevated neutral beige, which feels like a 2.0 version of the OG Perfectly Oversized Crewneck. I wore my heather gray Little Ribbed Tee underneath, which I’ve been wearing nonstop. It’s Lululemon’s take on a baby tee, but in a soft, ribbed fabric that looks just as good with denim as it does with a silk midi skirt. 

And because I love a matching set, I paired my cozy ‘fit with the French Terry Mid-Rise Short 3.5″, which are made from the same sturdy, matte French terry fabric. Think of them as a fancy, decidedly-not-grubby pair of sweats that wouldn’t look out of place at a luxe hotel spa—which is, conveniently, where I wore them for a post-race massage.

title: How To Dress Like Katseye, According To Your Fave Member Or Upcoming Concert
text:
How To Dress Like Katseye, According To Your Fave Member Or Upcoming Concert

From leather sets and polka dots to knee-high boots and plushies, there are many motifs now synonymous with Katseye’s unique aesthetic. The K-Pop girl group has already gone through several “eras,” or musical chapters, in their two-year career so far. But there’s no doubt that the “Pinky Up” single and accompanying music video cemented their place in the industry as global pop stars, and helped make each member recognizable by her first name alone, à la Addison. To dig deeper into this era’s aesthetic, I spoke with Katseye’s stylist Katie Qian to discuss the members’ cohesive yet chaotic looks and offer tips for fans (AKA Eyekons) who want to dress like Katseye for concerts, festivals, and more.

“The fans are obviously super dedicated on another level, so it makes me really happy when they like the looks and when they’re happy,” Qian tells Refinery29, adding: “From a styling perspective, we usually just focus on doing something that the girls and creative team loves, so when that lands, it’s great that the looks resonate with the people who love Katseye.”

Sharing how the aesthetic differs from the darker, edgier “Gnarly” era, Qian explains: “It’s really just about being fun and whimsical. There’s a lot of motifs in all the looks, like polka dots, always. There’s a bunch of fun textures like tulle and feathers. There’s this bustle element that we’re always bringing in. And then this rave element too of fun, chaotic, maximal layering.” She adds: “The girls love corsets, the girls love bras, and they love to feel sexy and cute.”

For Eyekons to channel the “Pinky Up” aesthetic, Qian suggests: “Any sort of way that the fans can play with what they have in their closet, honestly. Throw unconventional combinations together; mix different textures; and play with a lot of layering, fun cutouts, and asymmetry.” For more inspo, she adds: “The color scheme is usually blues, pinks, pastels, and also bright colors. And always add a wacky fun accessory — something that’s kind of kitschy and out of the box.”

In addition to Qian’s insights, I also took notes from a superfan (AKA my younger sister Sofia) for a breakdown of each member’s signatures that distinguish them from one another, from their style preferences to their cultural influences. Ahead, take inspo from some of Katseye’s most iconic looks since being styled by Qian in late 2025 for The Beautiful Chaos Tour through today with the launch of their Wild EP and new era. Then, shop key styles to put together concert outfits for their performance at Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields festival on August 29 or their WildWorld Tour starting on September 1.  

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Daniela

Lead-dancer Daniela Avanzini (22) comes from Atlanta, Georgia and embraces her Cuban and Venezuelan roots through her fashion and beauty choices. “I need to wear a cross, period. I feel like having a cross around my neck all the time… I feel protected. And it’s part of my childhood and my culture,” Daniela previously told Vogue in a Grammys getting-ready video, also citing seeing her mother wear hoops and reaching for them herself now. My sister also shares that she usually wears chunky sneakers paired with tiny tops and low-rise bottoms for a Y2K feel.

To channel Daniela, opt for edgy leather separates with lots of lace-up details, primary colors (if you’re not going for an all-black look), and chunky jewelry. She also predominantly opts for sets as opposed to bodysuits or dresses, so be sure to elevate your going-out bra top and hot pants game. For the final beauty touch, tightline your eyes with an intense inner eye and wear your hair curly or naturally.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Yoonchae

Yoonchae Jeung (18) serves as Katseye’s “maknae” or youngest member and comes from Seoul, South Korea, making her the only Korean in the K-Pop group. As the baby, she’s often dressed very cutesy, though has hints of a cool “tomboy” style. She told Vogue: “In the ‘Touch’ music video, I was wearing a triangle top and it became my thing,” with her styling team saying that fans always notice triangles on the torso of her outfits, which help give the illusion of an hourglass figure.

To get Yoonchae’s look, consider wearing scarf tops or voluminous mini skirts for an exaggerated hourglass silhouette. She’s often dressed in softer silhouettes, materials, and colors too, so opt for tulle, lace, and pinks when possible. To distinguish herself from her group members, Yoonchae also dyed her hair blonde for an extra light and soft beauty effect. So this may be your call to try the strawberry blonde hair color trend ASAP.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Lara

Main vocalist Lara Raj (20) was born in Connecticut but grew up in Texas and is of Indian and Sri Lankan descent. She brings her cultural identity into her style most prominently through jewelry via her bindis and tikkas, nose ring, and belly ring. “I make sure to go all out with my traditional stuff because it’s so important in that space where there’s so much press and so many photos and so many eyes on us to really represent my culture,” Lara told Vogue. The singer also notably wears many jewel tones and shimmering fabrics to complement her adornments.

Lara sticks to a few core necklines, like halters and sweetheart bra-cups across tops, bodysuits, and gowns, which highlight her chest tattoo. For accessories, if you’re not South Asian, a bindi or tikka may not be doable, but you can still implement crystal hair clips or face gems into your look instead. My sister also pointed out that the singer almost exclusively wears heels, so find a comfortable pair that you can dance the night away in.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Megan

All-rounder Megan Skiendiel (20) who has great range across singing and dancing also has the greatest range in style (and changing hairstyles). Originally from Honolulu, Hawaii, and of Chinese, Singaporean, and Swedish heritage, Megan has an equally varied approach to style. But she told Vogue: “For me, I usually wear my jade bracelet. I never take it off. I’ve had one since I was a kid so it’s a very big thing in Chinese culture.”

While Megan’s aesthetic evolves, she pretty consistently has the most alternative or edgy look, opting for dark eye makeup and hair highlights (including the viral “halo” hair trend). To channel Megan, keep to a color palette of black, white, purples, and reds. And in addition to a jade bracelet, you can also look out for a statement choker necklace, especially when paired with a bandeau-style neckline. Do something wild to your hair, and you’re set.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Sophia

As Katseye’s fan-dubbed leader, Sophia Laforteza (23) was raised in Manila, Philippines. While she’s currently on a wellness hiatus, she’s expected to return in September with more “Wild” era looks. As one of the oldest members of the group, my sister lovingly calls her “Mother,” and explains that Sophia’s style is a bit more sophisticated, polished, and modest at times. Pulling from coquette style, she typically wears lots of ruffles, rosettes, corsets, bloomers, and tulle.

Sophia also often wears halter crop tops across performance costumes and red carpet looks, so consider a halter for casual or fancy ‘fits. Amp up the volume with ruffle-sleeved tops or high-low skirts in pastels or vibrant pinks. Like Lara, Sophia typically prefers sleek heels instead of sneakers or boots, so step into pointy stilettos. And to finish off your look, layer on a juicy pink lip gloss before singing your heart out.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How To Dress Like Katseye’s Manon

Manon Bannerman (24), often described by fans as the group’s “visual,” has been on hiatus since February, but her signature aesthetic remains influential among Eyekons. Coming from Switzerland with a multicultural background, she pulls from her Ghanaian roots when it comes to fashion. “I always carry my waist beads with me. I got them in Ghana. It’s just a traditional thing we do in West Africa,” Manon told Vogue, adding: “They’re always on. Sometimes they’re hidden, but they’re like my lucky charm.”

Since we haven’t seen Manon’s take on the “Pinky Up” era, her style within the group is defined by the “Gnarly” era, where she leaned into darker palettes, metallics, lace-up corsets, chunky sneakers, and combat boots. Her ’90s minimalist look is paired back from too many accessories or jewelry — though you can try a waist chain — and is instead highlighted by her dramatic curly hair as the focal point.

title: Lululemon’s Big-Ass Bags Are Actually Kinda Brilliant
text:
Lululemon’s Big-Ass Bags Are Actually Kinda Brilliant

If your feed looks anything like mine, you might have noticed that there’s a new Lululemon drop causing a lot of commotion. No, it’s not another pair of leggings or an unexpected maxi skirt. This time it’s a Big-Ass carryall. That’s not me exaggerating the gargantuan measurements. That’s the actual name of the ludicrously capacious bag.

The banter online is hilarious, with some calling it the everything-AND-the-kitchen-sink bag. But seriously, as a person who hates going back and forth to the car after a grocery store run, this is the brilliant solution for lugging everything at once.

One review agrees, “This bag fits everything my family of 5 needs when traveling. My husband no longer complains about making multiple trips, carrying several bags.” While another one says, “Just throw this bad boy in the shopping cart, leave it open, and shop away! Makes Costco runs a breeze. Kinda wish it was bigger… although now I’m not sure how to get this 400 lbs bag into my car while I stand here in the parking lot… oh well! Lulu will you offer bigger sizes in the future? Thx.” Outside of the functional use cases, fashion has been pushing oversized bags to the forefront of the accessory department for a couple of seasons now.

Just look at Chanel’s Resort 2027 collection and you’ll find a colorful raffia tote that’s nearly the same size as the model carrying it. The intentionally exaggerated proportions were also seen at Altuzarra, Celine, and Stella McCartney—each one proving that it’s kinda chic to be a woman on the go carrying it all.

Of course, this isn’t Lululemon’s only bag that’s causing a frenzy. The girlies have been loving the wear-everywhere belt bags and adorable wristlets for years.

If you’re not quite ready for the 80L Big-Ass bag, Lululemon has some scaled-back versions that aren’t too big nor too small—like the Extra-Large and the Large Slouchy Shoulder Bag. Both of those styles are also perfect for days when you need to tote the necessities, while still ensuring you don’t overpack. Consider this your sign to add one of the durable, much-talked about bags to your collection.
